extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, legal practitioners, state agencies, and stakeholders affected by the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and statutory/administrative standards governing the FTC's final rule banning or restricting non-compete clauses, including who must receive notice, recordkeeping and contact-information practices, retroactivity limits, preemption of State law, and specific treatment of franchising and senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice required only for existing non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final rule, notice is only required for existing non-competes, i.e., those that have not elapsed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References in the final rule to § 910.2(b)(4)-(5) and related provisions; the Commission adopted a requirement that employers provide notice to workers who are bound by non-elapsed non-compete agreements so that workers know whether they remain (or wrongly believe they remain) subject to enforceable restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice is routine factual disclosure not implicating First Amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission notes that this required notice is a routine disclosure of valuable, factual information to workers that does not implicate the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Milavetz, Gallop & Milavetz, P.A. v. United States and Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel. The Commission adopted the notice requirement to ensure workers do not wrongly believe they remain bound by unenforceable non-competes, basing the conclusion on agency expertise and empirical evidence of an in terrorem effect related to non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers may use existing record-keeping to obtain contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers have many record-keeping requirements under State and Federal laws under which they may retain the contact information described in § 910.2(b)(2)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include IRS, Circular E, Employer's Tax Guide, Pub. 15 (retain employment tax records for at least 4 years, including addresses and forms with addresses) and USCIS Handbook for Employers M-274 (retaining Form I-9, which includes addresses, email addresses, and telephone numbers). This supports practical means for employers to provide the required notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance period defined
rubrics_metrics.description: The period between the publication of the final rule and the date on which compliance with the final rule is required is the 'compliance period.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM and final rule refer to this defined 'compliance period' (see NPRM at 3515). The Commission addresses compliance dates and timing (see proposed § 910.5 in the NPRM and Part VIII of the final rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule does not impose penalties or disabilities on pre-effective-date non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule imposes no penalties or other disabilities on persons who entered into non-competes before the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission explains that the final rule is designed not to attach penalties or new disabilities to pre-rule conduct, and addresses effective date issues in Part VIII. This limitation is part of the Commission's approach to avoid impermissible retroactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standard for retroactivity of administrative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative rule is retroactive only if it takes away or impairs vested rights acquired under existing law, or creates a new obligation, imposes a new duty, or attaches a new disability in respect to transactions or considerations already passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting courts: Regents of the Univ. of Cal. v. Burwell; Nat'l Min. Ass'n v. DOL; Landgraf v. USI Film Prods.; Nat'l Cable & Telecomms. Ass'n v. FCC. The Commission applies this legal standard to explain why the final rule is not treated as retroactive simply because it may 'impair the future value of past bargains' absent rendering past actions illegal or sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of part 910 limited to non-competes; not broad preemption of State antitrust/consumer-protection laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of part 910 is limited to non-competes. It would not broadly preempt other uses of State antitrust and consumer protection law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission emphasizes that part 910 targets non-competes specifically and does not override State antitrust or consumer protection enforcement more generally. The discussion references how other FTC rules address relations to State law and preemption and stresses limited scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws that afford equal or greater protection may not be preempted
rubrics_metrics.description: FTC regulations often exempt or preserve State laws that 'afford an overall level of protection that is as great as, or greater than, the protection afforded by' the FTC rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and textual formulations from prior FTC rules: Funeral Rule (16 CFR 453.9), Cooling-Off Period rule (16 CFR 429.2(b)), Business Opportunity Rule (16 CFR 437.9(b)), Franchise Rule (16 CFR 436.10(b)), Mail/Internet/Telephone Order Merchandise Rule (16 CFR 435.3(b)), and the Labeling and Advertising of Home Insulation (16 CFR 460.24(b)). Commenters suggested a similar formulation to allow existing State law to stand where protective levels are equal or greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchise-related non-competes and prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Franchise Rule requires franchisors to disclose any non-compete that franchisees must impose on managers. These non-competes are prohibited by the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 16 CFR 436.5(o)(3) and notes the final rule's treatment (see Parts III.D and V.D.6). The NPRM had excluded franchisees from the 'worker' definition in some contexts, but the final rule prohibits those franchisor-imposed non-competes on managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure rule for senior executives not adopted
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considered whether a disclosure rule would be appropriate for senior executives, but concludes that it is not because it would fail to address many of the ways in which non-competes are restrictive and exclusionary and tend to negatively affect competitive conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission explains that limiting a disclosure requirement to senior executives would not capture the full range of harms non-competes impose and therefore rejected a senior-executive-only disclosure approach (see discussion at NPRM/Final rule citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: NPRM proposed exclusions (franchisees and seller-buyer exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the NPRM, the proposed definition of 'worker' excluded franchisees in the context of franchisee-franchisor relationships; the NPRM also proposed an exception for certain non-competes between the seller and the buyer of a business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References NPRM at 3518-3520 and related discussion. The final rule's treatment of these proposed exclusions is discussed elsewhere in the final rule (see cross-references to Parts IV and III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission finds certain existing non-competes constitute unlawful unfair methods of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that the use of certain existing non-competes is an unlawful unfair method of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finding supports the Commission's view that the notice requirement does not run afoul of the First Amendment and forms part of the statutory basis under 15 U.S.C. 45 for the final rule (see Parts IV.B and C for findings on public benefits and harms).
